what_it_does: Flash storage chips (like those in USB drives or SSDs) can do simple logical operations directly on data sitting inside the chip — a technique called 'in-flash processing' — which avoids slow trips to move data out to the main processor and back. The catch is that existing in-flash processing can only combine data from cells that share a vertical wire (called a bitline); data on different vertical wires cannot interact, which rules out many useful operations like error-correction calculations and database filtering that inherently need to compare or combine values from different columns. CrossBit adds minimal extra circuitry to standard flash chips to create pathways between adjacent bitlines, enabling those cross-column operations for the first time in commodity flash hardware. This allows error-correction math (which needs to mix bits from many locations) and common database operations like selecting rows or joining tables to run inside the flash chip itself, without routing data all the way to an external processor.
